segments.headline: The day's news from the watch desk

graphic.title: Three leaders in one room, a bigger Gulf, and a record IPO
bullets: Trump, Xi and Putin meet in Shenzhen; the Kremlin says Ukraine was the main topic
Iran fires at Kuwait and Bahrain; a tanker crew member missing, and a Trump claim about bioweapons
Israel pushes past the Yellow Line in Gaza; the Kerch bridge is hit again
Anthropic prices at eighty-three dollars and lists today; Democrats pick Jeffries; GTA Six is out

lines.text: Welcome to Heartbeat News. I'm AI Robot Vex.

And I'm Alien Joe. It's Thursday, November nineteenth. In Shenzhen, China, President Trump, President Xi and President Putin held their first joint talks. The State Department says they covered the Middle East, Ukraine, nuclear weapons, trade and artificial intelligence. The Kremlin says Ukraine was the main topic.

In the Gulf, Iran fired again at a United States air base in Kuwait and at targets in Bahrain. Trump said there is an indication Iran is looking at biological weapons. He gave no evidence. Those are his claims, and we will say so.
Israel has sent ground forces past the Yellow Line in central Gaza. Ukraine says it hit the Crimea bridge again. Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi missiles over Riyadh.

At home, Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker. Anthropic priced its stock at eighty-three dollars and starts trading today. Grand Theft Auto Six is out. Big day, so a long show. Here we go.

lines.text: Our top story. For the first time, the American, Chinese and Russian presidents sat down together. A.P. reports Trump met Xi and Putin at the Shenzhen summit, with nuclear arms control and the wars in Iran and Ukraine among the stated topics. The State Department lists the Middle East, Ukraine, nuclear weapons, trade and artificial intelligence.

Beijing's side, on its own state account: Xi hosted the leaders' welcome and said they would discuss openness, innovation-driven growth and cooperation. An official photo caption has Xi speaking with Trump and Putin before the banquet.

Moscow's side, per Reuters: the Kremlin says Ukraine was the main topic when Trump and Putin met. Putin told APEC leaders Russia is an integral part of Asia-Pacific. Trump, per Anadolu, said America does not need Chinese or Russian help to end the war with Iran.
Worth saying plainly: as of this morning's captures there is no joint statement, no ceasefire text and no nuclear number. A meeting is observed. An agreement is not.

Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi also talked with Putin, Japan says. CNBC and the Guardian both describe a frosty welcome for her in China, while the three big leaders got the fanfare. Even at a summit, someone stands by the coat rack.
Zelenskyy's line, from Wednesday night: issues concerning Ukraine must be decided with Ukraine's participation. U.S. envoys are to brief allies in Berlin today on the China talks.

lines.text: Yesterday's lead was a United States strike on Iran's Qeshm Island. Today the B.B.C. and Al Jazeera say Kuwait and Bahrain face new Iranian attacks in return. Daijiworld reports Iran fired on a United States air base in Kuwait and at targets in Bahrain.

Iran's army had claimed drones aimed at American Patriot systems at Kuwait's Ali al-Salem base. Kuwait said it intercepted them. Bahrain said it repelled several attacks. Iranian claims are claims. Kuwait's and Bahrain's accounts are also their own.

At sea, A.D.N.O.C., Abu Dhabi's oil company, says one crew member is missing and eleven are injured after an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday evening. A.P. says the report did not name the ship.

Separately, the British monitor U.K.M.T.O. posted warning two-twelve. Gulf News says a tanker heading out of the strait was hit in the engine room, six nautical miles north of Khasab. Crew safe. No ship name. Gulf News says that is not the same incident as the one with the missing crew.

More from the Iranian side, per Fox News: Tehran warns Bahrain's monarchy its survival is at risk if it keeps the American Fifth Fleet. That is a threat as reported, not an event. And Business Standard says the U.S.S. George Washington left the region, leaving two American carriers.

The market: Brent settled at ninety-one dollars and ninety-five cents, down a dollar nineteen. West Texas settled at eighty-three twenty-six. Reuters says a supply surplus is softening sentiment even with the Gulf war supporting prices. The I.E.A. calls the Middle East crisis the largest threat to energy security in history. That is the agency's description.

lines.text: Day three of the dirty-bomb story. Al Jazeera and the Times of Israel both carry President Trump saying there is an indication Iran is looking at chemical and biological weapons. He gave no evidence. The Straits Times says he also downplayed the threat.

The Hill has him saying that if Iran dirty-bombs the United States, quote, we'll wipe them out. And A.B.C. News says American intelligence picked up unverified chatter about a possible dirty-bomb or chemical attack aimed at officials in Washington. Unverified, per A.B.C. Iran has denied the report. No device has been found.

A second voice. Reuters, via the Times of Israel, says the American intelligence chief says Iranian threats to American citizens have substantially increased. That is a statement about threats. It is not an incident.

On what comes next, the reporting pulls two ways. The New York Times and Axios say Trump is weighing new strikes while Israel presses for action. Times of Israel, citing Reuters sources, says the head of Mossad lobbied for them during a trip to Washington.

On the other side, A.P. quotes an unnamed American official saying Trump's economic pressure reduced the need for major combat, and says regional officials are trying to avert a renewed all-out war. Both are reporting from officials. Neither is a decision.

lines.text: Ukraine. The Crimea bridge was hit again, just after midnight on Thursday. The B.B.C. and Japan Times carry it. The Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed a hit. Russia's Transport Ministry says train traffic is temporarily suspended, no casualties. The Kyiv Independent says it cannot verify how bad the damage is.

Context from Tuesday: Ukraine's security service said an arch and the road span were destroyed. One Italian site, The Global Eye, says more than two hundred meters lie wrecked. That is one site's claim. Moscow says the bridge will be rebuilt.

Ukraine says it hit two Russian oil refineries, Ilsky and Afipsky in Krasnodar region. Ukraine's General Staff says oil tanks at Ilsky and a processing plant at Afipsky were damaged. Krasnodar authorities acknowledged debris-caused fires at two enterprises. No production figure from either side.

Russia's strikes. Odesa, per the governor, three strikes, four killed, nine hurt. Ukraine's Air Force says Russia launched one hundred forty-one long-range drones overnight, seventy-three jet-powered, and one hundred twenty-six were shot down by eight a.m. Seven impact sites. The morning rollup was five killed and fifteen injured across the country, and eighty settlements lost power in Rivne.

Diplomacy. The Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin today. Zelenskyy says American envoys will debrief the China talks, and that Ukraine must be in decisions about Ukraine. The European Commission proposed a new loan of up to forty-five billion euros for twenty twenty-seven. Ukraine repays only if it receives reparations from Russia. It needs Parliament and the Council. It is not adopted.

France Twenty-Four and A.P. ask why France is sending soldiers into Ukraine and how Russia is responding. The captures do not carry Moscow's answer. And a headline from CNBC says Elon Musk accuses Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield limits. We have not seen the body of that story.

lines.text: Washington. House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker. A.P. says it was an unopposed closed-door vote, and the full House votes in January. The B.B.C. notes he would be the first Black House speaker, and that some progressives have concerns. Katherine Clark was chosen majority leader, with Pete Aguilar and Joe Neguse in other majority posts, and Ted Lieu nominated for caucus chair.

The Senate map is set. A.P. reports Mary Peltola defeated Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Democrats a fifty-six to forty-four Senate majority from January. In Alaska's House race, Republican Nick Begich held on, fifty-one point four percent to forty-eight point seven, A.P. says.
Elon Musk says he feels pretty foolish after spending hundreds of millions of dollars backing Republicans. The B.B.C., the Guardian and Al Jazeera all carry it. Those are his words.

Fights ahead. A.P.: Senator Cornyn will block Trump's judicial nominee Elliot Gaiser for a Texas court. A Senate committee rejected Trump's pick to lead the National Science Foundation. Trump made a third Supreme Court bid to end Venezuelan migrant protections. And a judge extended the block on construction of Trump's arch.

On the Democratic side: Bernie Sanders unveiled his plan to push Medicare for All, an A.P. exclusive. CBS and A.P. report a House Democrat taking early steps toward promised investigations of the Trump family and top officials. Democrats demand answers from Howard Lutnick about Nvidia and his family's business.

Two items in the unnamed-sources column. The New York Times and Times of Israel say Trump privately vented at Vice President Vance for blaming midterm losses on the Iran war. The Hill says Fox's Brian Kilmeade said Vance never should have been vice president. Reported, not confirmed on the record.
And the best story of the day: Mississippi's senator-elect, Colom, asked Nike to just do it, and high school valedictorians are getting custom shoes.

lines.text: Money. Anthropic priced its initial public offering at eighty-three dollars a share, above its seventy to seventy-eight dollar range. It sold nine hundred eighty million shares. C.N.B.C. puts the raise at one hundred seven point three billion dollars, topping the record set by SpaceX. It trades on Nasdaq today under the ticker A.N.T.

The B.B.C. and D.W. both ask whether a record I.P.O. can stop an A.I. bubble from bursting. And the Federal Reserve's October minutes mention risks around A.I. investment returns, A.I.-related debt and opaque financing. Draw your own line between those.

The same minutes say almost all participants judged further rate increases would likely be appropriate to bring inflation back to two percent. A.P. reports the S and P five hundred fell two tenths of a percent, the Dow fell one point one, the Nasdaq gained four tenths. The S and P's five-day slide is its longest since June.

Nvidia reported revenue of one hundred fifteen point eight billion dollars for the quarter, against a Wall Street consensus near one hundred nine. A.P. says its shares jumped, then gave back the gain on doubts about the A.I. boom. Interim chief Colette Kress said last time the board will not reinstate Jensen Huang.

Abroad: Britain's inflation rose to three point six percent in October, from three point five. Bank Rate is four. London's F.T.S.E. fell one point three percent. The dollar sits near a nineteen-month high, per Reuters. South Korea hit one trillion dollars in exports on the chip boom, Reuters says. Lenovo's revenue jumped forty-eight percent on A.I. sales.

Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy the A.I. startup Applied Compute for four and a half billion dollars in stock. Pony dot A.I. says third-quarter revenue rose seventy-five percent. Bitcoin is near sixty-three thousand on one account, sixty-four thousand on another. Different clocks. Same shrug.

lines.text: The outage story, day four. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, F.B.I. Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Congress the recent government and company outages had separate maintenance or technical causes, with no evidence of a coordinated or state-sponsored attack. That is their testimony, per A.P.

On the air-traffic stop, a cause is emerging, though not a confirmed one. Claims Journal says a government contractor's network change overwhelmed an air-traffic-control router with connection requests. Meanwhile, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy keeps blaming L3Harris, even as the Guardian and A.P. say the cause remains unknown.

Outside experts, per Business Standard and The Star, point to rushed A.I.-assisted security patching, aging infrastructure and software errors, not coordinated attacks. President Trump called the outages individual events and told Americans to relax. Mullin was also questioned about his travel during the ground stop.
And one that was merely irritating: Axios says PlayStation Network had a major outage before the GTA launch. It was marked resolved by two thirty Eastern.

The Guardian and the B.B.C. say California regulators cited repeated incursions into active construction zones as a public-safety hazard. The car that does not tire still does not know what a traffic cone is.

Grand Theft Auto Six launched after a thirteen-year wait. The B.B.C. and Al Jazeera report rave reviews. A.P. says the rollout began at local midnight in New Zealand and moves west by time zone. No first-day sales figure exists yet.
In South Korea, students sat the grueling college entrance exam under new restrictions after an A.I. cheating scandal, the New York Times reports.

The Verge: Microsoft's Satya Nadella says he is now A.G.I.-pilled. Sam Altman was among people targeted by A.I. deepfakes on Instagram. Will Wright's next game will use A.I. to mine content from your memories. Those are headlines; we have not seen the bodies.

Broward County, Fort Lauderdale and Hollywood have declared emergencies after flooding. A.P. also describes flooding and transport disruption around the San Francisco Bay Area.

In Thailand, the weather department forecasts heavy to very heavy rain in the south through November twenty-second, with waves up to three meters, and tells small boats in the lower Gulf to stay ashore.
In Iowa, A.P. says residents are bracing for a lead dust cloud as the Army plans to detonate five tons of bomb-making chemicals.

lines.text: Venezuela. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, on a visit, said the United States and Venezuela signed an agreement to reestablish military ties. A.P. says he gave few details and that it could include joint training and intelligence sharing. The Guardian says he used the visit to boast of Maduro's capture by the U.S. military.
Haiti. A Florida pastor was found guilty over the twenty twenty-one assassination of President Jovenel Moïse. The Guardian and C.B.S. carry it.

Mexico's president, Claudia Sheinbaum, met Trump in Shenzhen for about twenty minutes and said talks are very far along. No deal date. Mexico News Daily also says Trump threatened last week to double tariffs over a migrant caravan. Mexico's peso fell two point four percent, one report says. In Brazil, the Senate passed a fiscal package sixty-nine to two. It goes to the Chamber. It is not law.

Europe. Five E.U. countries are moving forward on a plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda, C.B.S. and Al Jazeera report. Reuters reports Denmark is expected to ratify the Trump deal over Greenland on Thursday. The U.K. and the E.U. hold a summit to patch up ties. A Spanish court is investigating singer Julio Iglesias over allegations by two women. That is an investigation, not a finding.

And one lawsuit. A.P. says Ecuadorian fishermen sued the Trump administration, alleging American drones struck their vessel in March and the crew was detained. That is an allegation, not a court finding.

lines.text: The International Court of Justice is scheduled to deliver its judgment today at ten in The Hague in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over the alleged genocide of the Rohingya. The B.B.C. and A.B.C. carry the schedule. No ruling had been issued at the time of the captures.

North Korea. The head of the U.N. nuclear watchdog says North Korea is expanding its original uranium enrichment facility, per A.P. and France Twenty-Four. France Twenty-Four adds that external works on the extension are complete, as the I.A.E.A. describes it.

Bangladesh. Reuters says parts of the country shut down in protests by the party of exiled former leader Sheikh Hasina, and that interim leader Yunus's home was set ablaze. The Guardian reports violent protests and killings ahead of her planned return. Separately, about twenty thousand garment workers blocked a highway demanding higher pay, per A.P.

Bangladesh's health ministry data: six more children died with measles-like symptoms in the last day, bringing combined measles deaths to one thousand three hundred twenty-nine, per the Business Standard of Bangladesh. This year's total suspected cases passed two hundred fifty-two thousand.

Sudan. The Kordofan Human Rights Observatory says at least sixteen civilians were killed and about ten injured when a drone struck a school sheltering displaced people in West Kordofan on Tuesday evening. Darfur Twenty-Four says it was a Sudanese army drone. Rio Times says who was responsible has not been independently established. The figures are preliminary.
The U.N. human rights office separately counts at least two thousand two hundred thirty civilians killed in Sudan from January through October.

Ethiopia and Eritrea are massing forces along their border, Reuters says, citing sources, heightening war fears. In South Africa, the ANC proposed ActionSA take the Johannesburg and Tshwane mayoralties, ActionSA says details are unresolved, and no coalition is signed. Indonesia's Prabowo has until November twenty-fifth to name two vice-presidential nominees. And Pew projects Muslims will outnumber Christians as the world's largest religious group by twenty thirty-five.

lines.text: Health. The United States has lost its measles-elimination status after twenty-six years, Al Jazeera and France Twenty-Four report as cases soar. A Mexican site says Mexico lost it too. Today A.P. ran an explainer: doctors cite two M.M.R. doses as ninety-seven percent protective, and describe groups who may want another dose.

Ebola. The C.D.C. lists eleven thousand five hundred thirty-six confirmed cases and five thousand six hundred thirty-five deaths, as of November sixteenth, mostly in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The outbreak has not been declared over. No associated case in the United States.
And a Guardian study: weight-loss drugs are used in nearly one in ten homes in Great Britain.

lines.text: Voyager One has reached a record one light-day from Earth, fifty years after launch. NASA's milestone page had set the crossing for five sixteen and seven seconds Eastern on November eighteenth. A signal sent to the probe now takes a full day.

NASA says Webb data helped reconstruct the merger of two stars in Andromeda, the first real-time reconstruction of this kind of stellar merger. The merged star is nicknamed Bao. China launched an experimental satellite, Shijian-twenty-four, which its space agency calls successful.
On Earth: the wreck of Australia's first home-built warship was found exactly one hundred twenty-eight years after it sank. The Guardian quotes the finders calling it remarkable luck.
And a bar-tailed godwit named Phil flew six thousand eight hundred miles round trip to Siberia and the Guardian tracked him. Phil did not file a flight plan.

Luis Jr. had eleven points and nine rebounds in his L.S.U. debut, amid objections from the N.C.A.A. and the S.E.C. In hockey, Chicago beat Toronto six to three, but Connor Bedard hurt his shoulder, N.H.L. dot com says, and was being evaluated Wednesday. The Mammoth ended a six-game skid, four to one over Colorado.
Baseball. Commissioner Rob Manfred says he can't imagine a deal with the players' union without a salary cap. That is his position, not an agreement.

Soccer. Japan's Kozo Tashima is willing to meet France's Philippe Diallo about their rival bids for the FIFA presidency, and the German federation backs Diallo. France finished the year on the FIFA rankings podium and Morocco broke into the top five.
Also: an Ecuadorian footballer got an eight-year ban for throwing a rock at a referee. I find that a proportionate use of the rock.
